newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Gold plunge cuts ground from under Australia miners.
newsitem.headline: Gold plunge cuts ground from under Australia miners.

text.p: Australia's gold miners are facing a crisis as grave as any in living memory as they struggle to live with the effects of a slump in the price of the yellow metal.
Analysts estimate up to 55 percent of the gold mined in Australia is produced at a total cost above the current market price -- a situation that will soon start to take its toll.
"Small, high-cost producers are the ones that are going to go to the wall first and that's going to happen pretty fast," Bell Securities gold analyst Keith Goode told Reuters.
Based on March quarter production figures, Goode believes about 30 percent of the Australia's gold production was produced at a cash cost above the current spot price.
Ironically, the trigger for gold's recent fall was Australia's central bank which announced late last week it had sold 167 tonnes of its gold reserves in the past six months.

Gold was fetching around US$317 per ounce (A$427) in Asian trading on Tuesday, but has fallen below US$315, its lowest price in 11-1/2 years. It was trading at around US$332 before news broke of the Australian sales.
The situation for Australia's gold sector is even grimmer on the stock market with the Australia Stock Exchange's (ASX) gold index plummetting 16 percent in the past three trading sessions.
Sandra Close, head of mining consultant Surbiton Associates, said the situation was serious but about half the industry still had its head above water.

"About 55 percent of Australia's gold output is produced at a cash cost below the current spot gold price. On a total cost basis, we estimate that about 40-45 percent of gold is produced below the current price," she said.
Close said miners could cut costs by mining high grade ore and cutting exploration budgets but this was not sustainable.
"High-grading shortens mine life, reduced development leads to production problems in the future and less exploration reduces the discovery rate of new deposits," Close said.

Bell Securities' Goode said large miners would be able to survive in the medium term because of established hedging arrangements but smaller producers without substantial hedge positions would suffer quickly.
"Forward sales average out for the industry around about the one-and-a-half to two year period - that's the cushion. It depends how much further (the gold price fall) goes beyond that," he said.

John MacDonald, gold analyst at Perth broker, Eyres Reed MacIntosh said hedging gave some financial protection but miners still had to reference their mines to the Australian dollar spot price for gold.
"If you are being hard-nosed, hedging doesn't protect your mines -- it protects your company. It is financial insurance not mining insurance," MacDonald said.

A survey of gold producers undertaken earlier this year found Australian miners had the world's highest costs. Costs have been pushed up by the fact that many Australian mines have exhausted surface supplies and must dig ever deeper.
Gold Fields Mineral Services Ltd's study of the world gold industry found the average cash cost of world gold production in 1996 was US$262 per ounce.
This compared to Australian miners' average cash cost of US$292 an ounce and total average costs of US358 per ounce.
Australian gold production costs are expected to remain under pressure due to a possible capping of the diesel fuel rebate scheme for miners.

Also miners in Western Australia, which produce about 70 percent of Australia's gold, were recently hit by the intoduction of a 1.25 percent royalty on production, increasing to 2.5 percent in 1999/2000.
-- Melbourne Bureau 61-3 9286-1435
